title: Topic-based lexical mastery: how to use the 15 topics
blocks: p

The fifteen domains in this chapter are the topics IELTS returns to again and again. Whatever the exact question, your Task 2 essay and your Speaking answers will draw on this vocabulary. Each topic gives you a complete bundle: ten academic nouns, ten precise verbs, ten collocations and adjectives, five formal collocations built for Writing Task 2, and five natural idioms built for Speaking.
p

The line between the last two matters enormously, and Chapter 5 is devoted to it; here, simply notice that the formal set is labelled for Writing and the idiom set for Speaking, and keep them apart. Work each topic, then do its three exercises before checking the answers. A note on the Bangla glosses: they give the everyday meaning of each academic noun so the term is anchored to something you already know.
p
Do not translate word for word into your essays; use the English term in its natural collocation.

title: Topic 1 · Environment and Climate Shift
blocks: h2
Academic nouns (10)
ul
**emission** (নিঃসরণ): Industrial emissions are a leading driver of global warming.
**deforestation** (বন উজাড়): Widespread deforestation has accelerated the loss of natural habitats.
**biodiversity** (জীববৈচিত্র্য): The destruction of wetlands threatens the region’s biodiversity.
**ecosystem** (বাস্তুতন্ত্র): Even small changes in temperature can disrupt a fragile ecosystem.
**degradation** (অবক্ষয়): Soil degradation reduces agricultural productivity over time.
**sustainability** (টেকসইতা): Long-term sustainability must guide national energy policy.
**conservation** (সংরক্ষণ): The conservation of freshwater resources is now an urgent priority.
**pollutant** (দূষক): Vehicle exhaust releases harmful pollutants into the atmosphere.
**depletion** (নিঃশেষ হওয়া): The depletion of fossil fuels has intensified the search for alternatives.
**carbon footprint** (কার্বন পদচিহ্ন): Individuals can reduce their carbon footprint by using public transport.
h2
Precise verbs (10) · past, participle, -ing
ul
**emit** (emitted, emitted, emitting): Factories emit large quantities of greenhouse gases.
**deplete** (depleted, depleted, depleting): Overfishing has depleted marine stocks worldwide.
**mitigate** (mitigated, mitigated, mitigating): Reforestation can mitigate the effects of climate change.
**conserve** (conserved, conserved, conserving): Households should conserve water during the dry season.
**pollute** (polluted, polluted, polluting): Untreated waste continues to pollute major rivers.
**degrade** (degraded, degraded, degrading): Intensive farming gradually degrades the soil.
**offset** (offset, offset, offsetting): Companies can offset emissions by funding tree planting.
**preserve** (preserved, preserved, preserving): Protected areas help preserve endangered species.
**exploit** (exploited, exploited, exploiting): Nations must stop exploiting natural resources recklessly.
**contaminate** (contaminated, contaminated, contaminating): Chemical runoff can contaminate groundwater.
h2
Collocations and adjectives (10)
ul
**renewable energy**: Investment in renewable energy is rising steadily. (Writing)
**fossil fuels**: We remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. (Writing)
**environmentally friendly**: Many consumers now prefer environmentally friendly products. (Speaking and Writing)
**a pressing environmental concern**: Air quality has become a pressing environmental concern. (Writing)
**greenhouse gas emissions**: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires global cooperation. (Writing)
**irreversible damage**: Rising sea levels could cause irreversible damage to coastlines. (Writing)
**carbon neutral**: Several cities aim to become carbon neutral by 2050. (Writing)
**finite resources**: Water and oil are finite resources that must be managed carefully. (Writing)
**eco-friendly** (Speaking): I try to make eco-friendly choices, like carrying a reusable bottle. (Speaking)
**climate change** (adjective use, climate-related): Climate-related disasters are becoming more frequent. (Writing)
h2
Formal Task 2 collocations (5) · Writing
ul
**pose a serious threat to**: Rising temperatures pose a serious threat to food security.
**at the expense of**: Economic growth should not come at the expense of the environment.
**strike a balance between**: Governments must strike a balance between development and conservation.
**have a detrimental impact on**: Plastic waste has a detrimental impact on marine life.
**take collective action**: Only collective action can address the climate crisis effectively.
h2
Speaking idioms and expressions (5) · Speaking only
ul
**a drop in the ocean**: Recycling at home helps, but it is a drop in the ocean compared with industry. (Part 3)
**the tip of the iceberg**: The visible pollution is just the tip of the iceberg. (Part 3)
**go green**: More families are trying to go green these days. (Part 1)
**weather the storm**: Coastal communities have to weather the storm of frequent flooding. (Part 3)
**a breath of fresh air**: Escaping to the countryside is a real breath of fresh air. (Part 2)

blocks.title: Exercise 4.1.3 · Speaking Simulation Drill
blocks.instructions: Answer each Part 3 question in two to three sentences, using at least one target idiom and one collocation. Then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: What can ordinary people do to protect the environment?
items.answer: Ordinary people can go green in small ways, such as cutting their carbon footprint by using public transport, though individual effort alone is only a drop in the ocean without industrial reform.

items.prompt: Do you think individual effort is enough to solve climate change?
items.answer: Individual effort matters, but on its own it is a drop in the ocean; without governments taking collective action and industries cutting emissions, personal choices cannot reverse the damage.

items.prompt: How might cities become more environmentally friendly in the future?
items.answer: In future, cities could become far greener by investing in public transport, expanding green spaces, and adopting renewable energy, which together would shrink their carbon footprint.

title: Topic 2 · Education and Pedagogy
blocks: h2
Academic nouns (10)
ul
**curriculum** (পাঠ্যক্রম): A modern curriculum should balance theory with practical skills.
**pedagogy** (শিক্ষণবিদ্যা): Effective pedagogy adapts to the needs of individual learners.
**literacy** (সাক্ষরতা): Improving adult literacy is a key development goal.
**assessment** (মূল্যায়ন): Continuous assessment reduces the pressure of a single final exam.
**enrolment** (ভর্তি): University enrolment has risen sharply over the past decade.
**discipline** (শৃঙ্খলা): Self-discipline is essential for successful independent study.
**attainment** (অর্জন): Educational attainment is closely linked to future income.
**vocation** (বৃত্তি): Vocational training prepares students for specific trades.
**aptitude** (দক্ষতা / সহজাত ক্ষমতা): Standardised tests attempt to measure academic aptitude.
**scholarship** (বৃত্তি / শিক্ষাবৃত্তি): Scholarships enable talented students from poor families to study.
h2
Precise verbs (10) · past, participle, -ing
ul
**enrol** (enrolled, enrolled, enrolling): Thousands of students enrol in online courses each year.
**acquire** (acquired, acquired, acquiring): Children acquire language most easily when young.
**cultivate** (cultivated, cultivated, cultivating): Good schools cultivate curiosity, not just obedience.
**assess** (assessed, assessed, assessing): Teachers assess progress through regular feedback.
**foster** (fostered, fostered, fostering): Group projects foster teamwork and communication.
**memorise** (memorised, memorised, memorising): Rote learning encourages students to memorise rather than understand.
**specialise** (specialised, specialised, specialising): Undergraduates specialise in their chosen field in later years.
**motivate** (motivated, motivated, motivating): Skilled teachers motivate even reluctant learners.
**broaden** (broadened, broadened, broadening): Travel broadens young people’s understanding of the world.
**equip** (equipped, equipped, equipping): Practical training equips graduates with job-ready skills.
h2
Collocations and adjectives (10)
ul
**higher education**: Access to higher education has widened considerably. (Writing)
**critical thinking**: Universities should develop students’ critical thinking. (Writing)
**well-rounded education**: A well-rounded education includes arts as well as sciences. (Writing)
**lifelong learning**: The modern economy demands lifelong learning. (Writing)
**academic performance**: Sleep has a direct effect on academic performance. (Writing)
**student-centred**: A student-centred approach places learners at the heart of the lesson. (Writing)
**compulsory education**: Compulsory education should last until at least sixteen. (Writing)
**hands-on experience**: Internships give students valuable hands-on experience. (Speaking and Writing)
**rote learning**: Rote learning has limited long-term benefit. (Writing)
**highly qualified**: The school employs highly qualified teachers. (Speaking and Writing)
h2
Formal Task 2 collocations (5) · Writing
ul
**lay the foundation for**: Early schooling lays the foundation for later success.
**bridge the skills gap**: Vocational courses help bridge the skills gap in industry.
**equip students with**: Education should equip students with practical, transferable skills.
**place emphasis on**: Some systems place too much emphasis on examinations.
**broaden one’s horizons**: Studying abroad can broaden a young person’s horizons.
h2
Speaking idioms and expressions (5) · Speaking only
ul
**learn the ropes**: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes at university. (Part 2)
**a steep learning curve**: The first year of my degree was a steep learning curve. (Part 2)
**pass with flying colours**: She passed her final exams with flying colours. (Part 1)
**hit the books**: Before exams, I really have to hit the books. (Part 1)
**think outside the box**: Good teachers encourage you to think outside the box. (Part 3)

blocks.title: Exercise 4.2.3 · Speaking Simulation Drill
blocks.instructions: Answer each Part 3 question in two to three sentences, using at least one target idiom and one collocation. Then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: Do you think exams are the best way to assess students?
items.answer: Exams measure knowledge under pressure, but they reward rote learning over critical thinking, so continuous assessment often gives a fairer picture of a student’s real attainment.

items.prompt: How important is a university degree in today’s job market?

items.prompt: Should schools focus more on practical skills or academic knowledge?

title: Topic 3 · Technology and Automation
blocks: h2
Academic nouns (10)
ul
**automation** (স্বয়ংক্রিয়করণ): Automation has replaced many routine factory jobs.
**innovation** (উদ্ভাবন): Constant innovation keeps the technology sector growing.
**connectivity** (সংযোগ ব্যবস্থা): High-speed connectivity has transformed rural businesses.
**surveillance** (নজরদারি): Digital surveillance raises serious concerns about privacy.
**algorithm** (অ্যালগরিদম): Social media algorithms decide what users see.
**infrastructure** (অবকাঠামো): Reliable digital infrastructure is now essential for the economy.
**obsolescence** (অপ্রচলন): Rapid obsolescence forces consumers to replace devices often.
**integration** (সংহতকরণ): The integration of technology into classrooms is uneven.
**artificial intelligence** (কৃত্রিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা): Artificial intelligence is reshaping many professions.
**digital divide** (ডিজিটাল বৈষম্য): The digital divide leaves poorer communities behind.
h2
Precise verbs (10) · past, participle, -ing
ul
**automate** (automated, automated, automating): Firms increasingly automate repetitive tasks.
**innovate** (innovated, innovated, innovating): Companies that fail to innovate quickly fall behind.
**streamline** (streamlined, streamlined, streamlining): New software has streamlined the ordering process.
**integrate** (integrated, integrated, integrating): Schools are integrating tablets into daily lessons.
**revolutionise** (revolutionised, revolutionised, revolutionising): The smartphone has revolutionised communication.
**facilitate** (facilitated, facilitated, facilitating): Video calls facilitate remote collaboration.
**hack** (hacked, hacked, hacking): Criminals can hack poorly protected networks.
**upgrade** (upgraded, upgraded, upgrading): Users must regularly upgrade their software.
**disrupt** (disrupted, disrupted, disrupting): Streaming services have disrupted the film industry.
**monitor** (monitored, monitored, monitoring): Employers can monitor staff activity online.
h2
Collocations and adjectives (10)
ul
**cutting-edge technology**: The lab uses cutting-edge technology. (Speaking and Writing)
**user-friendly**: A user-friendly interface encourages wider adoption. (Writing)
**data privacy**: Data privacy has become a major public concern. (Writing)
**technological advancement**: Technological advancement has boosted productivity. (Writing)
**screen time**: Excessive screen time may harm children’s development. (Speaking and Writing)
**remote working**: Remote working became widespread after the pandemic. (Writing)
**tech-savvy**: Younger users tend to be more tech-savvy. (Speaking)
**digital literacy**: Digital literacy is now as vital as reading and writing. (Writing)
**state-of-the-art**: The hospital installed state-of-the-art scanners. (Writing)
**highly automated**: Modern warehouses are highly automated. (Writing)
h2
Formal Task 2 collocations (5) · Writing
ul
**transform the way we**: The internet has transformed the way we access information.
**at the click of a button**: Vast amounts of data are available at the click of a button.
**render obsolete**: Automation may render many manual jobs obsolete.
**raise ethical concerns**: Artificial intelligence raises significant ethical concerns.
**bridge the digital divide**: Affordable devices can help bridge the digital divide.
h2
Speaking idioms and expressions (5) · Speaking only
ul
**glued to the screen**: Teenagers are often glued to their screens. (Part 3)
**cutting corners**: Some firms cut corners on cybersecurity. (Part 3)
**a double-edged sword**: Social media is a double-edged sword. (Part 3)
**keep up with the times**: Businesses must keep up with the times to survive. (Part 3)
**at your fingertips**: These days, information is at your fingertips. (Part 1)

items.prompt: Has technology made our lives easier or more complicated?
items.answer: Technology is a double-edged sword: information is now at our fingertips, which makes life easier, yet many people end up glued to their screens, which complicates it.

items.prompt: Do you think automation will create more jobs than it destroys?

title: Topic 4 · Health and Modern Lifestyles
blocks: h2
Academic nouns (10)
ul
**obesity** (স্থূলতা): Rising obesity is straining public health systems.
**nutrition** (পুষ্টি): Good nutrition in childhood shapes lifelong health.
**wellbeing** (সুস্থতা / কল্যাণ): Mental wellbeing deserves the same attention as physical health.
**epidemic** (মহামারী): Diabetes has reached epidemic levels in many countries.
**prevention** (প্রতিরোধ): Prevention is far cheaper than treatment.
**sedentary lifestyle** (নিষ্ক্রিয় জীবনযাপন): A sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of heart disease.
**immunity** (রোগ প্রতিরোধ ক্ষমতা): Vaccination builds immunity against serious diseases.
**healthcare** (স্বাস্থ্যসেবা): Universal healthcare remains a distant goal in many nations.
**addiction** (আসক্তি): Screen addiction is a growing concern among the young.
**longevity** (দীর্ঘায়ু): Better healthcare has increased human longevity.
h2
Precise verbs (10) · past, participle, -ing
ul
**alleviate** (alleviated, alleviated, alleviating): Exercise can alleviate mild anxiety.
**prevent** (prevented, prevented, preventing): Regular checkups help prevent serious illness.
**diagnose** (diagnosed, diagnosed, diagnosing): Doctors can now diagnose many conditions earlier.
**combat** (combated, combated, combating): Public campaigns combat the spread of misinformation about health.
**boost** (boosted, boosted, boosting): A balanced diet boosts the immune system.
**deteriorate** (deteriorated, deteriorated, deteriorating): Without treatment, the patient’s condition may deteriorate.
**recover** (recovered, recovered, recovering): Most patients recover fully with rest.
**transmit** (transmitted, transmitted, transmitting): The virus is transmitted through close contact.
**treat** (treated, treated, treating): Antibiotics treat bacterial infections effectively.
**maintain** (maintained, maintained, maintaining): Regular exercise helps maintain a healthy weight.
h2
Collocations and adjectives (10)
ul
**a balanced diet**: A balanced diet is the foundation of good health. (Speaking and Writing)
**mental health**: Mental health has finally entered public debate. (Writing)
**life expectancy**: Life expectancy has risen across the developing world. (Writing)
**chronic illness**: Chronic illness places a heavy burden on families. (Writing)
**physically active**: Staying physically active reduces many health risks. (Speaking and Writing)
**preventive measures**: Simple preventive measures can save lives. (Writing)
**health-conscious**: Consumers are becoming more health-conscious. (Speaking)
**fast food**: A diet high in fast food contributes to obesity. (Speaking and Writing)
**public health**: Air pollution is now a public health emergency. (Writing)
**well-balanced**: A well-balanced routine includes rest and exercise. (Writing)
h2
Formal Task 2 collocations (5) · Writing
ul
**place a strain on**: An ageing population places a strain on healthcare services.
**take a toll on**: Long working hours take a toll on mental health.
**lead a sedentary lifestyle**: More people now lead a sedentary lifestyle.
**promote a healthy lifestyle**: Schools should promote a healthy lifestyle from an early age.
**the root cause of**: Poor diet is often the root cause of preventable disease.
h2
Speaking idioms and expressions (5) · Speaking only
ul
**as fit as a fiddle**: My grandfather is eighty but as fit as a fiddle. (Part 1)
**under the weather**: I was feeling under the weather all last week. (Part 1)
**burn the candle at both ends**: Students often burn the candle at both ends during exams. (Part 3)
**on the mend**: She was ill but is now on the mend. (Part 2)
**prevention is better than cure**: When it comes to health, prevention is better than cure. (Part 3)

items.prompt: Whose responsibility is it to keep people healthy, the individual or the government?

title: Topic 5 · Crime, Justice and Rehabilitation
blocks: h2
Academic nouns (10)
ul
**deterrent** (প্রতিরোধক): Long sentences are intended to act as a deterrent.
**rehabilitation** (পুনর্বাসন): Rehabilitation aims to reintegrate offenders into society.
**recidivism** (পুনরায় অপরাধ প্রবণতা): High recidivism suggests that prison alone does not work.
**offender** (অপরাধী): First-time offenders are often given lighter sentences.
**surveillance** (নজরদারি): Public surveillance has reduced street crime in some cities.
**corruption** (দুর্নীতি): Corruption undermines public trust in institutions.
**penalty** (শাস্তি): The penalty for drug trafficking is severe.
**victim** (ভুক্তভোগী): Support services help victims recover from trauma.
**legislation** (আইন প্রণয়ন): New legislation targets online fraud.
**justice system** (বিচার ব্যবস্থা): An efficient justice system must be both fair and swift.
h2
Precise verbs (10) · past, participle, -ing
ul
**deter** (deterred, deterred, deterring): Harsher penalties may deter potential criminals.
**rehabilitate** (rehabilitated, rehabilitated, rehabilitating): Programmes that rehabilitate offenders reduce reoffending.
**prosecute** (prosecuted, prosecuted, prosecuting): The state prosecuted the company for fraud.
**reoffend** (reoffended, reoffended, reoffending): Many released prisoners reoffend within a year.
**enforce** (enforced, enforced, enforcing): Police must enforce the law consistently.
**impose** (imposed, imposed, imposing): Courts can impose fines or imprisonment.
**commit** (committed, committed, committing): Young people sometimes commit crimes out of desperation.
**combat** (combated, combated, combating): New units were formed to combat cybercrime.
**convict** (convicted, convicted, convicting): The jury convicted him of theft.
**safeguard** (safeguarded, safeguarded, safeguarding): Strong laws safeguard citizens’ rights.
h2
Collocations and adjectives (10)
ul
**capital punishment**: Capital punishment remains a divisive issue. (Writing)
**community service**: Minor offences may be punished with community service. (Writing)
**law-abiding**: Most citizens are law-abiding. (Speaking and Writing)
**crime rate**: The crime rate has fallen in recent years. (Writing)
**repeat offender**: Repeat offenders face longer sentences. (Writing)
**petty crime**: Petty crime rises when unemployment is high. (Writing)
**zero tolerance**: The city adopted a zero-tolerance policy on vandalism. (Writing)
**behind bars**: The offender spent five years behind bars. (Speaking)
**white-collar crime**: White-collar crime often goes unpunished. (Writing)
**wrongful conviction**: A wrongful conviction can ruin an innocent life. (Writing)
h2
Formal Task 2 collocations (5) · Writing
ul
**act as a deterrent**: Severe penalties can act as a deterrent to crime.
**address the root causes**: Reducing crime means addressing its root causes, such as poverty.
**reintegrate into society**: Rehabilitation helps offenders reintegrate into society.
**uphold the law**: An independent judiciary is needed to uphold the law.
**impose strict penalties**: Governments should impose strict penalties on corporate fraud.
h2
Speaking idioms and expressions (5) · Speaking only
ul
**get away with it**: Some criminals get away with it for years. (Part 3)
**take the law into your own hands**: People should not take the law into their own hands. (Part 3)
**a slap on the wrist**: A small fine is just a slap on the wrist. (Part 3)
**turn over a new leaf**: After prison, he turned over a new leaf. (Part 2)
**crack down on**: The authorities are cracking down on drink-driving. (Part 3)

blocks.title: Exercise 4.5.3 · Speaking Simulation Drill
blocks.instructions: Answer each Part 3 question in two to three sentences, using at least one target idiom and one collocation. Then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: Is prison the best way to deal with criminals?
items.answer: Prison can act as a deterrent, but on its own it does little to lower recidivism; programmes that rehabilitate offenders and help them turn over a new leaf tend to work better in the long run.

items.prompt: Do you think the causes of crime are mainly social or individual?
items.answer: The causes are largely social; crime often stems from poverty and a lack of opportunity, so addressing the root causes tends to be more effective than harsh punishment alone.

items.prompt: Should minor crimes be punished with community service instead of prison?
items.answer: For minor offences, community service is often preferable, because it helps offenders reintegrate into society and turn over a new leaf rather than hardening them behind bars.
